stimuli.description: Four office test environments: wood and plants, wood and no plants, no wood and plants, and no wood and no plants. Wood furniture had birch veneer with a clear finish. Non-wood furniture had white painted and melamine foil surfaces. Plants included Chlorophytum comosum (spider plant), Dracaena marginata (variegated red), and Schefflera actinophylla (Amate). Non-plant items were a blue glass vase, plastic inbox/outbox filer, and a stand fan. The view to the outside was blocked by closed blinds. The PASAT test was an auditory stressor.

limitations: No treatment or stressor effects found for HRV, possibly due to no real differences or undetected differences by chosen methodologies.
Baseline stress level was sufficiently high that it did not allow for parasympathetic dominance in any period.
Time spent habituating to the environment was not enough to engage the parasympathetic system.
Sitting position of subjects may have prevented HRV from being present or detectable.
2.5-minute epochs may not have been sufficient to capture HRV (5-minute epochs suggested).
Quality issues with some ECG records due to data collection from wrists instead of torso, potentially introducing more noise.
PASAT test was an acute stressor, which may not accurately characterize chronic stress in office environments.
PASAT caused subjects to stop looking at their surroundings, counteracting the study's goals.
Limited plant surface area in the study precludes conclusions on the effect of plants on stress.
Uncertainty whether observed effects are a positive effect of wood or a negative effect of man-made/artificial surfaces (e.g., melamine).
Melamine may have negative connotations, though unlikely to be a factor given its common use and lack of consumer awareness of the term.
PASAT is not a conventional measure of attention for environmental psychology, and mathematical ability was a confounding factor.
Single-blind experiment: experimenter awareness of study goals could lead to unintentional non-verbal cues influencing subjects.
Visible outside light entered the room from between the blinds, and differences in ultraviolet light were not controlled for.
Potential for a history confound as all non-wood rooms were run first, though no evidence for serial or history effects was found.
Wood/non-wood effect could be a response to color, as wood inherently has yellow-red hues not formally controlled against white furniture.
